+# Pitch runbook — 2026-08-28
+
+Investor-facing pitch decks and delivery runbook for the four ideas that won the
+tournaments in [`../expanding-frontiers-tournament-2026-08-28/`](../expanding-frontiers-tournament-2026-08-28/)
+and [`../expanding-frontiers-whitespace-and-youth-2026-08-28/`](../expanding-frontiers-whitespace-and-youth-2026-08-28/).
+
+| File | What it is |
+|---|---|
+| `RUNBOOK.md` | The whole thing: four decks, elevator pitches, why-it-helps, slide-by-slide, anticipated questions, kill criteria, and the delivery runbook. |
+| `SOURCE_REGISTER.md` | Sources S30-S37 with confidence grades, plus obligations O13-O16. |
+
+## The four decks
+
+| Deck | Idea | Elevator pitch | Ask |
+|---|---|---|---|
+| 1 | **Boom Baseline** | Every major airport continuously measures its own noise. Not one spaceport does. | $750K pre-seed, or a $250K design-partner contract |
+| 2 | **Peninsula** | A $12B LNG export terminal and a methane-fuelled orbital launch site now share one peninsula, and no model exists for what one does to the other. | $500K, or two paid pilot studies |
+| 3 | **SARGO** | The Gulf took 5 million metric tons of sargassum in a single month, Texas pays to shovel it off the beach, and 30 km away is a launch site that runs on methane. | $1.5M seed, or $400K non-dilutive to kill the arsenic question |
+| 4 | **The Boom Map** | Every airport measures its noise. No spaceport does. I built the first one, on my street. | Mentorship, an internship, and $2K of sensors |
+
+## Two rules the whole runbook is built on
+
+**Say the weak thing first.** Each idea has one genuine hole and each deck names it on
+its own slide: Boom Baseline has no confirmed payer, Peninsula looks like consulting,
+SARGO has arsenic, The Boom Map is a high school project. An investor who finds an
+undisclosed hole stops trusting the true parts of the deck too.
+
+**Grade every number, and cut every C.** A, B or DERIVED goes on a slide. C does not.
+The market sizing is deliberately a ladder of graded figures rather than a single TAM,
+because a fabricated TAM is the fastest way to lose a technical investor, and
+"the analogous market is $343M a year and spaceport spend is zero" is a stronger
+sentence than an invented multiplication.
+
+## Presentable version
+
+`brownsville-decks.html` is the same four decks rendered as a standalone page, published as an artifact at
+https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0f93c2f6-7b30-4fe8-b3cc-099e12ffc886 . `RUNBOOK.md` remains the source of

+# Pitch Runbook — four ideas, investor audience
+
+Companion to the tournaments in
+[`../expanding-frontiers-tournament-2026-08-28/`](../expanding-frontiers-tournament-2026-08-28/)
+and [`../expanding-frontiers-whitespace-and-youth-2026-08-28/`](../expanding-frontiers-whitespace-and-youth-2026-08-28/).
+Sources are cited as `S<n>` against those directories' registers, plus `S30-S37`
+added here in `SOURCE_REGISTER.md`.
+
+| Deck | Idea | Stage | Ask |
+|---|---|---|---|
+| 1 | **Boom Baseline** | Pre-seed venture | $750K pre-seed, or a $250K design-partner contract |
+| 2 | **Peninsula** | Pre-seed venture | $500K pre-seed, or two paid pilot studies |
+| 3 | **SARGO** | Pre-seed / grant-stage deep tech | $1.5M seed, or $400K non-dilutive to kill the arsenic question |
+| 4 | **The Boom Map** | High school project | Mentorship, an internship, and $2K of sensors |
+
+---
+
+## Part 0 — Read this before you pitch anything
+
+### The audience change, and what it costs you
+
+The tournaments optimised for an Expanding Frontiers grant panel. **Investors score a
+different rubric**, and three of your best grant arguments become liabilities in front
+of them:
+
+| Grant panel rewards | Investor asks instead |
+|---|---|
+| Regional economic impact, RGV jobs | "Does the market exist outside Brownsville?" |
+| NASA technology basis | "Do you own anything, or are you licensing what anyone can license?" |
+| Non-dilutive capital efficiency | "What does this look like at $50M of revenue?" |
+| Community benefit | "Who signs the cheque, and how often?" |
+
+So each deck below is rebuilt around the four questions an investor actually asks:
+**who pays, how much, how often, and why can't someone else do it.** The regional
+material stays, but demoted to a "why we win here first" slide rather than the thesis.
+
+### The rule that governs all four decks
+
+**Say the weak thing first.** Every one of these ideas has one genuine hole, named in
+its deck. An investor who finds a hole you did not disclose stops trusting everything
+else in the deck, including the parts that are true. An investor who watches you name
+your own hole and show the plan to close it is evaluating a founder, which is what they
+are actually doing anyway.
+
+Boom Baseline's hole is that no payer is confirmed. Peninsula's is that it looks like
+consulting. SARGO's is arsenic. The Boom Map's is that it is a high school project.
+None is fatal. All four are fatal if concealed.
+
+### Numbers discipline
+
+Every figure in these decks is graded. **A** = primary or corroborated. **B** = single
+credible source. **C** = weak, do not put on a slide. **DERIVED** = arithmetic on other
+figures, with the assumption stated out loud.
+
+If you cannot say which grade a number is, take it off the slide.
+
+---
+
+# Deck 1 — Boom Baseline
+
+> **The measurement layer every airport has and no spaceport does.**
+
+## Elevator pitch
+
+**One line:** Every major airport continuously measures its own noise. Not one
+spaceport does. We build that layer, starting at the busiest launch site in America.
+
+**Thirty seconds:** Airport noise monitoring is a $343 million a year market because
+airports learned decades ago that you cannot grow operations a community does not
+trust. Spaceports never built it. Now the FAA projects launch and reentry operations
+going from about 330 a year to over 1,000 by 2030 and 10,000 by 2035, and the first
+launch community in America has taken its operator to federal court. We deploy
+calibrated, independently operated overpressure and acoustic monitoring around launch
+sites and sell the record to everyone who currently has to argue without one: the
+operator, the spaceport authority, the regulator, the insurer and the county.
+
+## Why it helps, and who it helps
+
+This is the slide that separates you from a grievance project. **The record helps the
+operator most.**
+
+| Who | What they have today | What the record gives them |
+|---|---|---|
+| Launch operator | Predictions that were wrong by 1 to 4 psf on one measured flight (S22), and a lawsuit | A defensible, third-party number; the ability to prove a mitigation worked |
+| Spaceport authority | Anecdote | The instrument every airport authority already runs (S23) |
+| FAA | Models with a measured miss (S22), and a mandate to license 30x more operations (S32) | Ground truth to calibrate against |
+| Insurer / county | No basis to price or adjudicate | Actuarial data |
+| Residents | A courtroom | A number |
+
+Airports did not solve community noise by winning arguments. They solved it by
+measuring, publishing, and making the number the shared reference. That is the
+business.
+
+## The deck, slide by slide
+
+**1. Title.** Boom Baseline. *The independent measurement layer for launch communities.*
+One image: a launch, and a house, in the same frame.
+
+**2. The problem.** Launch cadence in populated areas is now limited by public consent,
+and consent is being negotiated with no shared instrument. Around 80 plaintiffs across
+roughly 60-70 households in Port Isabel and South Padre Island are in federal court
+over eleven tests between April 2023 and October 2025 (S21, grade A). Nobody in that
+dispute, including the operator, has a continuous calibrated record.
+
+**3. Why now.** Three things became true at once, and none was true five years ago:
+- FAA projects over 1,000 licensed launches and reentries a year by 2030 and 10,000 by 2035, from about 329 worldwide in 2025 (S32, grade A/B). That is roughly a 30x increase.
+- The FAA opened rulemaking on **siting new spaceports** in August 2026 (S33, grade B). More launch sites near more people is now policy, not speculation.
+- The first community-versus-operator case is live (S21), so the cost of having no number just became visible to everyone.
+
+**4. The insight.** *Spaceports are where airports were before noise monitoring was
+standard.* Toronto Pearson runs 25 permanent IEC 61672 Class 1 terminals streaming
+continuously (S23, grade A). Envirosuite alone serves over 200 environmentally
+constrained airports (S30, grade B). At spaceports this market is $0.
+
+**5. The product.** A network of calibrated overpressure and acoustic nodes, an
+independently held chain-of-custody record, and a published method anyone can attack.
+We measure **what arrived**. We never claim what it caused. That restraint is the
+product: a number both sides can use is worth more than a number one side likes.
+
+**6. Market.** Presented as a ladder, with the honest grade on each rung:
+
+| Rung | Figure | Grade |
+|---|---|---|
+| Analogous market today: airport noise monitoring systems | $342.5M (2025), $366.9M (2026), $579.8M (2034) | B |
+| Wider environmental noise monitoring | $2.4B (2025) to $4.6B (2034), 7.5% CAGR | B |
+| Launch sites globally | 80 orbital and suborbital | B |
+| FAA-licensed US spaceports | 14 (9 horizontal, 4 vertical) | A |
+| Spaceport community monitoring today | **$0** | A |
+| Operations growth to 2035 | ~329/yr (2025) to a projected 10,000/yr | A/B |
+
+**Say this out loud:** "I am not going to divide a market figure by a site count and
+call it a TAM. The honest statement is that the analogous market is $343 million a
+year, the asset class is 80 sites growing under a federal siting rulemaking, the
+operations that drive the need are projected to grow 30x, and the current spend is
+zero. Price discovery is the first thing your money buys."
+
+**7. Business model.** Per-site annual monitoring subscription plus an installation
+fee, with a data licence for insurers and authorities. Recurring, infrastructure-shaped,
+and it grows with cadence rather than with headcount.
+
+**8. Traction.** Be exact about what exists and what does not. Today: the analysis, the
+site relationships, and a costed deployment plan. In 90 days: a calibrated reference
+network capturing real events. There is a cheaper proof running in parallel, described
+in Deck 4, which produces a real dataset for about $2,000.
+
+**9. Moat.** Not the sensors, which are commodity. Three things: the **longitudinal
+calibrated record**, which cannot be back-filled by a competitor arriving later; the
+**independence**, which the operator structurally cannot self-supply for a dispute it
+is party to; and the **method**, published and defended in public until it becomes the
+reference.
+
+**10. The ask.** $750K pre-seed for 18 months: reference network at one site, first
+published record, price discovery, and two paid pilots. Alternative on the same slide:
+a $250K design-partner contract, which we prefer, because a customer is better than a
+cheque.
+
+**11. Use of funds.** Roughly: 40% deployment and calibration, 25% engineering, 20%
+commercial and price discovery, 15% legal, consent and data policy.
+
+## Anticipated questions
+
+**"Who actually pays? Name them."** *The honest answer, delivered first:* not yet
+confirmed, and it is the first thing this round resolves. The candidate payers are the
+operator, the spaceport authority, the county, insurers and the FAA. The airport
+analogy says the operator or the authority pays, because that is who pays at airports.
+I will not tell you I have a signed customer when I do not. What I will tell you is that
+30 days of price discovery is the first milestone and you can hold me to it.
+
+**"Won't SpaceX just publish their own data and kill you?"** They may, and it would be
+a real competitive event. It does not settle the dispute, for the same reason airports
+do not self-certify community noise: the value is independence, and an operator's own
+number is not usable by a party in dispute with the operator. Also note what happened
+when the prediction was tested: measured overpressures exceeded FAA predictions by one
+to four psf (S22). Self-reported modelling is exactly what lost credibility.
+
+**"This is a lawsuit support business."** No, and I will not build one. Same data, same
+terms, to every party including the operator. The moment the record is for sale to one
+side, its value collapses to zero, because the other side stops accepting it. That is a
+commercial argument, not an ethical pose.
+
+**"Sensors are commodity. What stops a competitor?"** Correct, and the sensor is not
+the product. The product is a calibrated chain-of-custody record with a published
+method and a longitudinal series. A competitor starting in 2028 cannot produce 2026 data.
+
+**"Is this venture scale or a lifestyle business?"** Honest answer: unproven, and it
+depends entirely on whether per-site contract values look like airport contracts. If
+they do, 80 sites growing under a federal siting rulemaking is a real business. If they
+do not, this is a public-good programme and you should not fund it. That is a
+falsifiable question and it is milestone one.
+
+**"Why you?"** Because the work is already specified, the site relationships are local,
+and the cheapest possible proof is already designed and running at student scale for
+about $2,000. Ask me again after the reference network is up.
+
+**"What if the FAA mandates it and a big incumbent takes it?"** That is the good
+outcome for the market and the dangerous one for us, so we sequence for it: be the
+published method and the incumbent record before a mandate lands. Envirosuite got there
+in aviation by being early, not by being biggest.
+
+**"Regulatory risk?"** The primary risk is the opposite of the usual one: we need the
+FAA to care more, not less. The August 2026 siting rulemaking (S33) points that way.
+Verify its current status before you rely on it.
+
+**"Privacy exposure from measuring private homes?"** Real, and handled before any
+deployment: written consent per site, publication aggregated by street or larger, no
+address ever identifiable. This is a live workstream, not a slide.
+
+## Kill criteria
+
+Walk away if: someone is already doing calibrated community monitoring at a spaceport;
+or no payer of any kind will state a number after 60 days of trying; or the only
+willing payer is a litigation funder.
+
+---
+
+# Deck 2 — Peninsula
+
+> **Two industries that have never been neighbours are now neighbours, and nobody owns the risk between them.**
+
+## Elevator pitch
+
+**One line:** A $12 billion LNG export terminal and a methane-fuelled orbital launch
+site now share one peninsula, and no model exists for what one does to the other.
+
+**Thirty seconds:** Process safety is a mature discipline with mature vendors, and every
+one of them models a facility against its own hazards and its own fence line. Nobody
+models a facility against a *neighbouring facility of an entirely different industry*
+with a different regulator, because until now that pairing did not exist. Rio Grande
+LNG comes online in 2027 about 12 miles from Starbase, the FAA is opening rulemaking on
+siting more spaceports, and the co-location problem is about to repeat. We build the
+cross-facility quantitative risk model for that new asset class, and sell it to both
+sides plus their insurers and regulators.
+
+## Why it helps
+
+Each operator today can answer "what happens if my facility has an event." Neither can
+answer "what happens if *theirs* does," and neither regulator asks: FERC and PHMSA
+govern the terminal, the FAA governs the launch site, and the boundary between them is
+nobody's jurisdiction. Everyone in that gap is exposed and knows it.
+
+## The deck, slide by slide
+
+**1. Title.** Peninsula. *Cross-facility risk for co-located critical infrastructure.*
+
+**2. Problem.** Quantitative risk assessment stops at the fence line. Co-location of
+dissimilar high-consequence facilities creates hazard paths that neither operator's
+model contains and neither regulator reviews.
+
+**3. Why now.** Rio Grande LNG, roughly $12B and about 1,000 acres, targeted to operate
+in 2027, about 12 miles from Brownsville and adjacent to an orbital launch site (S12,
+grade A). Texas LNG is a second project in the same area. The FAA opened rulemaking on
+siting new spaceports in August 2026 (S33, grade B). This pairing is not a one-off; it
+is the beginning of a pattern.
+
+**4. Product.** A cross-facility quantitative risk model delivered as software plus a
+maintained model subscription, not as a consulting report: shared hazard paths, joint
+consequence modelling, cross-operator emergency response, and cryogenic road transport
+routing through populated corridors.
+
+**5. Market.** Comparables are the process safety and QRA vendors, DNV and the
+specialist consultancies. The new asset class is co-located launch and energy
+infrastructure, which today is a handful of sites and, under the siting rulemaking,
+a growing one. **State honestly that this is a small market today.**
+
+**6. Business model.** Model build fee, then annual model maintenance as facilities
+change. Sell to both operators, their insurers, and the authorities.
+
+**7. Moat.** The first cross-facility model becomes the reference other parties argue
+against. Regulatory acceptance compounds.
+
+**8. Ask.** $500K, or preferably two paid pilot studies.
+
+## Anticipated questions
+
+**"This is consulting with extra steps."** The fairest attack, and the answer has to be
+structural: the deliverable is a maintained model with a subscription, not a report;
+revenue recurs because facilities change; and the second model costs far less than the
+first because the hazard library carries over. If we cannot demonstrate that by the
+second engagement, you are right and this should not be venture funded.
+
+**"You need facility data from two operators who will not give it to you."** Correct,
+and it is the hardest gate. Two routes: start from public filings, FERC, PHMSA and FAA
+environmental documents, and build the model that is defensible without proprietary
+data; or enter through the insurer, who can require the data neither operator will
+volunteer. The tournament scored this idea's startability at 3 out of 10 for exactly
+this reason and I am not going to pretend otherwise.
+
+**"Why won't DNV just do this?"** They can and might. They are organised by industry
+vertical, which is precisely why the cross-vertical gap exists. That is a real but
+temporary advantage measured in a couple of years.
+
+**"How big can this get?"** Small today. It scales only if co-location becomes common,
+which is what the siting rulemaking suggests but does not guarantee. If you need a
+billion-dollar outcome, this is not it.
+
+## Kill criteria
+
+Walk away if neither operator nor any insurer will engage after two quarters, or if a
+defensible model cannot be built from public filings alone.
+
+---
+
+# Deck 3 — SARGO
+
+> **We get paid to take the feedstock, and the contaminant everyone else treats as the obstacle is the product.**
+
+## Elevator pitch
+
+**One line:** The Gulf just took 5 million metric tons of sargassum in a single month,
+Texas pays about $2.9 million a year to shovel it off the beach, and 30 km away there is
+a launch site that runs on methane.
+
+**Thirty seconds:** Sargassum is the rare feedstock with a negative acquisition cost:
+municipalities already pay to remove it. It anaerobically digests into methane. The
+reason nobody has built a real business on it is arsenic, which the seaweed
+bioaccumulates and which poisons both the digester's performance and the digestate's
+downstream use. Everybody treats that as the obstacle. We treat it as the moat: solve
+contaminant separation and you own a fuel business and a remediation business at the
+same time, in the one place on earth that has record blooms, LNG liquefaction
+infrastructure and a methane-fuelled launch customer within one county.
+
+## Why it helps
+
+Three parties currently pay for the same problem and get nothing back: coastal
+municipalities pay to landfill it, tourism loses revenue to it, and a launch operator
+buys methane trucked in from elsewhere. One process addresses all three.
+
+## The deck, slide by slide
+
+**1. Title.** SARGO. *Negative-cost feedstock. Contaminant separation as the moat.*
+
+**2. Problem, sized.** The Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt hit a record 37.5 million tons
+in 2025 (S34, grade B). In June 2026 the Gulf of Mexico alone hit about 5 million metric
+tons, nearly double its previous record, with the eastern Caribbean at about 9 million
+(S34, grade B). Texas spends roughly $2.91 million a year on beach removal; Miami-Dade
+has estimated about $35 million a year (S35, grade B). EPA and the Texas General Land
+Office both run inundation programmes (S36, grade A).
+
+**3. The economics nobody else gets.** Feedstock cost is **negative**. You are paid to
+accept the input. That is the same structural advantage landfill-gas and dairy RNG
+projects built businesses on, and it is rare.
+
+**4. Why nobody has done it — say this before they ask.** Arsenic. Sargassum actively
+bioaccumulates it, because its phosphate transporter confuses arsenic for phosphate.
+Arsenic is elevated in fresh biomass and released during decomposition. Digestate
+carries arsenic and zinc requiring treatment before agricultural use, and heavy metals
+may cause toxicity that further reduces methanogenic performance (S27, grade A). Methane
+yield is modest, around 92.62 mL CH4 per gram of volatile solids (S26, grade B). And
+Caribbean and Mexican groups are already commercialising general sargassum valorisation
+(S28, grade A), so the general idea is not even novel. **Only the contaminant-first
+framing and the Texas propellant pairing are.**
+
+**5. The thesis.** If arsenic is why the field is empty, then arsenic separation is the
+company. Two products from one process: pipeline or propellant-grade biomethane, and a
+remediation and clean-digestate stream that unlocks the agricultural market everyone
+else's digestate is locked out of.
+
+**6. Why here.** Record Gulf blooms, existing LNG liquefaction infrastructure within
+the county, and a methane-consuming launch customer about 30 km from the beach (S12,
+S13). No other coastline has all three.
+
+**7. Business model.** Tipping fees on intake, offtake on biomethane, and licensing the
+separation process. Three revenue lines, the first of which starts before the technology
+is proven.
+
+**8. Ask.** $1.5M seed, or $400K non-dilutive to answer one question: can arsenic be
+separated at a cost that leaves the fuel economic. **That question is the whole company.**
+
+## Anticipated questions
+
+**"Isn't the yield too low to matter?"** Probably, on fuel alone, at published yields.
+The model does not close on fuel revenue by itself, which is why tipping fees and the
+remediation product are not garnish. If your thesis needs fuel-only economics, pass.
+
+**"Arsenic sounds like a research programme, not a startup."** For the first 12 months
+it is, which is why the preferred ask is non-dilutive. Fund the question, not the
+factory. If arsenic separation does not work at cost, we will tell you and stop.
+
+**"Caribbean groups are already doing this."** They are doing valorisation broadly
+(S28). Nobody is doing contaminant separation as the primary product, and nobody is
+pairing it to a propellant customer. If that turns out to be wrong, the differentiation
+is gone and so is the investment case.
+
+**"Seasonality?"** Blooms are seasonal and volatile between years, so intake and
+storage economics are a real design constraint, not a footnote. 2026 came in second to
+2025 rather than setting a new record (S34), which tells you the variance is large.
+
+**"Regulatory path for arsenic-bearing waste?"** Unresolved and material. Handling and
+disposal classification could change the economics substantially. It belongs in
+diligence, and I am flagging it rather than waiting for you to find it.
+
+## Kill criteria
+
+Walk away if arsenic separation cost exceeds the combined tipping plus fuel plus
+remediation revenue at pilot scale, or if the waste classification makes handling
+uneconomic.
+
+---
+
+# Deck 4 — The Boom Map
+
+> **A high school student builds the dataset a venture-funded company does not have yet.**
+
+**Read the audience carefully.** For this deck "investors" are competition judges,
+programme sponsors and mentors, and the currency is not equity. But there is a genuine
+investor angle, and it is the strongest thing about this project: **The Boom Map is the
+cheapest possible proof of Boom Baseline's core assumption.** For about $2,000 it tests
+whether a distributed sensor network around a launch site produces a coherent,
+publishable gradient. A venture investor should care about that, because it is a
+seven-figure question being answered for four figures.
+
+## Elevator pitch
+
+**One line:** Every airport measures its noise. No spaceport does. I built the first one,
+on my street.
+
+**Thirty seconds:** I live in Port Isabel. When Starship launches, my house shakes, and
+so do my neighbours'. Right now the only measurements anyone has are a few academic
+studies and an argument in federal court. I built fifteen sensors, put them on my
+neighbours' homes and my school with their written permission, and published the first
+public map of what each launch does to each street. Every major airport has run this
+kind of network for decades. Not one spaceport has. I made the first one.
+
+## Why it helps
+
+The community gets a number instead of an argument. The school district finds out what
+its buildings actually take. Researchers get open data nobody else has. And the launch
+operator gets something it currently lacks: an independent record it can point to when
+it says a mitigation worked.
+
+## The deck, slide by slide
+
+**1. Title.** The Boom Map. *The first independent record of what a launch does to a
+neighbourhood.* Photograph of a sensor on a real house.
+
+**2. Why me.** I live here. My house is one of the data points. That is not a
+qualification anyone can buy, and it is the reason the neighbours said yes.
+
+**3. The gap.** Toronto Pearson runs 25 permanent certified noise terminals (S23).
+Every major airport does something similar. Searching for the equivalent at any
+spaceport turns up test labs and one-off academic studies, not a network (S24).
+
+**4. What I built.** Fifteen nodes across Port Isabel and South Padre at different
+distances from the pad, plus one in the school. Under $500 of hardware. Calibrated
+against each other to a measured, documented tolerance.
+
+**5. What I found.** The map, the gradient with distance, the raw data published
+openly, and the method written so another student can repeat it.
+
+**6. What I am careful about, and this is the important slide.** Written consent from
+every homeowner before installation. No address is ever published; everything is
+aggregated by street. These are not laboratory-grade instruments and I say so. And I
+measure what **arrived** at a house. I make no claim about what caused any damage to
+any house. That distinction is the difference between science and an accusation.
+
+**7. What is next.** A full year of data, which nobody else on earth would have. Open
+publication. And a build guide so students at other launch sites can run the same
+network.
+
+**8. What I need.** Mentorship on calibration methodology, an internship where I can
+learn to do this properly, and about $2,000 to extend to 40 nodes and a year of
+operation.
+
+## Anticipated questions
+
+**"Did you really do this yourself?"** Bring the build log, the calibration
+spreadsheet, and the failures. Show a node that did not work and explain why. Nothing
+proves authorship like a well-documented mistake.
+
+**"Isn't this just anti-SpaceX?"** No, and here is the test: I am giving the same data
+to everyone, including them, on the same terms. If they can show a mitigation reduced
+overpressure on my street, my network is how they prove it. A community that trusts the
+number is how launch cadence goes up, not down.
+
+**"Your sensors aren't calibrated to standard."** Correct. They are consumer-grade,
+cross-calibrated against each other to a documented tolerance, and I publish that
+tolerance. They establish relative gradient and repeatability, not certified absolute
+levels. That limitation is on my slide, not hidden in my notes.
+
+**"What if there's no launch during your project window?"** Then my result is a
+deployed, calibrated, documented network and a build guide, which is still a real
+result, and I will present it that way rather than pretending otherwise.
+
+**"How is this a business?"** For me right now it is not, and I would rather be honest
+about that than dress up a science project. It is the beginning of the dataset a real
+company would need, and if it turns into one, the year of data is what makes it
+defensible.
+
+**"What about your neighbours' privacy?"** Written consent before every install,
+aggregation by street, never an address. I wrote that policy before I built the first
+sensor.
+
+## Runbook for the student
+
+- **Consent before hardware.** Write the one-page consent form first. A judge notices.
+- **Start on your own house.** No permission needed, and a working node is what convinces
+  the first neighbour.
+- **Eight sites is the floor.** Below that it is data points, not a map.
+- **Publish the raw data.** Openness is the entire credibility of the project.
+- **Same entry, three venues.** ExF Space Entrepreneur Summer Academy, the Conrad
+  Challenge (ages 13-18) and the Diamond Challenge take this with no rework (S20, S29).
+- **Never say your house was damaged by a launch.** Say what your sensor measured. Let
+  the number speak.
+
+---
+
+# Part 5 — Questions every investor will ask all four
+
+**"Why hasn't anyone done this?"** Have the specific answer per idea, and never say
+"nobody thought of it." Boom Baseline: the precondition, launch cadence near people, is
+new. Peninsula: the space is gated behind two operators' data. SARGO: arsenic. Naming
+the real reason is what makes the whitespace credible instead of suspicious.
+
+**"How do you know nobody is doing it?"** The honest answer: "We searched patents, SBIR
+and STTR awards, trade press, FAA filings and county records, and found nothing. That is
+a negative search result, not proof. If you know of someone, tell me now and it changes
+my plan today." An investor who hears that respects it. One who hears "nobody is doing
+it" assumes you did not look.
+
+**"What is your unfair advantage?"** For three of these four the honest answer is
+location and timing, not proprietary technology. Say it. Then say what converts it into
+a durable one: the longitudinal record, the first regulator-accepted model, the
+separation process.
+
+**"What kills this?"** Have the kill criteria memorised. Founders who can state the
+conditions under which they would stop are the ones investors believe about everything
+else.
+
+**"How much have you validated with customers?"** Currently: not enough. Do not
+inflate it. Say what you have, say what the next 30 days buys, and offer to report back.
+
+---
+
+# Part 6 — Delivery runbook
+
+**Before the room**
+- Grade every number on your slides A, B or DERIVED. Remove every C. The AFRL programme
+  figures and any prize amount from a prior cycle are C.
+- Rehearse the weak slide until it is your calmest one.
+- Bring one physical object. A sensor node in a plastic enclosure beats a rendering.
+- Prepare the one-page leave-behind: elevator pitch, the ask, the kill criteria, contact.
+
+**In the room**
+- Lead with the gap, not the technology. "Every airport does this. No spaceport does."
+- Name your hole by slide six at the latest. Do not let them find it at slide ten.
+- When you do not know, say "I don't know, and here is how I would find out." It scores
+  higher than a confident guess and it is the only answer that survives diligence.
+- Never claim causation from measurement. Never claim a licence you have not signed.
+  Never present a projection as a finding.
+
+**After the room**
+- Send the leave-behind within 24 hours with one new fact you did not have in the room.
+- Log every question you could not answer. Those questions are your next milestones,
+  and the pattern across several pitches is more useful than any single meeting.
+
+**Never do these**
+- Never build or imply a plaintiff-side positioning for Boom Baseline or The Boom Map.
+  It destroys the product's value, which is that both sides accept the number.
+- Never publish data identifying a specific property.
+- Never let a minor near cryogens, rocket hardware, industrial property or restricted land.
+- Never claim the whitespace is proven. It is a search result until someone disproves it.

+# Expanding Frontiers Award Tournament — Full Investigation Report
+
+Run date: 2026-08-28. Base commit: `59a5364` (`main`).
+Method: `prompts/shared/ULTIMATE_SOLUTION_TOURNAMENT.md` executed with the SUBJECT
+"which venture idea most likely wins a grant or award from Expanding Frontiers."
+Machine-readable results: `TOURNAMENT_RESULTS.json` (regenerate with
+`python docs/plan/expanding-frontiers-tournament-2026-08-28/score_tournament.py`).
+Evidence and its limits: `SOURCE_REGISTER.md`.
+
+---
+
+## 0. The answer
+
+| Rank | Idea | Weighted | One line |
+|---|---|---|---|
+| **1** | **Frontier Assurance** | **8.79** | A sealed flight recorder for autonomous operations. Tamper-evident, independently re-executed proof of what an uncrewed system actually did, wedged into offshore booster recovery and cryogenic propellant transfer. |
+| 2 | CryoAssay | 8.02 | Propellant-grade LNG certification and boil-off loss accounting for the Brownsville cryo corridor, with a NASA integrated-refrigeration licence as the hardware second act. |
+| 3 | Saltline | 6.84 | Startup-NASA-licensed corrosion and thermal-protection coatings qualified for a decommissioned Gulf platform deck that must survive both salt spray and rocket exhaust. |
+
+Verdict: **ADAPT**, not adopt. The winner is a hybrid that did not exist before the
+tournament. Neither of the two strongest originals wins unmodified.
+
+Confidence: **medium, and deliberately not higher.** The scoring criteria are
+*derived* from what Expanding Frontiers is documentably rewarded for, not quoted
+from a published rubric, and obligations O1-O7 in `SOURCE_REGISTER.md` are open.
+The sensitivity analysis in section 2.1 shows the result is not robust to a rubric
+change: **under a hardware-favouring rubric CryoAssay wins instead**, and with the
+founder-advantage criterion removed the two are effectively tied (margin 0.078).
+Read rank 1 and rank 2 as "prepare both, submit the one the real rubric rewards".
+Settling which is node `EF-000`, the first thing to do.
+
+---
+
+## 1. Subject interpretation
+
+The naive reading of this request is "find three good space startup ideas." That
+reading loses. Expanding Frontiers is not a venture fund; it is a 501(c)(3)
+ecosystem builder whose own funding — an EDA STEM Talent Challenge award, a
+$50,000 DOE EPIC Prize, a 2025 SBA Growth Accelerator Fund award in the *Capital
+Formation* category — is justified to its funders on Rio Grande Valley economic
+development and NASA technology commercialisation (S1, S5, S6, S7).
+
+That changes the objective function. ExF wins when its portfolio creates
+high-paying RGV jobs and pulls federal non-dilutive dollars into South Texas. A
+judging panel selecting on that basis will pass over a technically superior idea
+that could be executed from Boulder in favour of one that must be executed within
+sight of the Brownsville ship channel. The tournament is therefore scored on
+**probability of winning this specific award from this specific organisation**,
+not on venture quality.
+
+Second constraint, equally load-bearing: the flagship prize is a reported $32,000
+split across three business plans (S2). That is not a number that de-risks
+hardware. It funds a design partner, a field trial, a licence application, or a
+credible prototype. Any idea whose next honest milestone costs seven figures is
+asking the wrong funder, and the scoring reflects that.
+
+---
+
+## 2. The evaluation system (GenericPrompt section 4)
+
+Built for this subject, not inherited from a template. Ten criteria, weights
+summing to 1.0:
+
+| Criterion | Weight | Why it carries this weight |
+|---|---|---|
+| `mission_fit_space_energy` | 0.14 | ExF's signature thesis is Rockets & Rigs: problems *common to* space and energy (S4, S5). A dual-sector idea is not a bonus here, it is the house specialty. |
+| `rgv_regional_anchor` | 0.13 | Every dollar ExF has raised was justified on regional development. Portability is a defect in this contest. |
+| `customer_proximity_30km` | 0.13 | Starbase, Rio Grande LNG, Texas LNG, the Port of Brownsville and the reported AFRL recovery headquarters sit inside one commute. A named local buyer beats a TAM slide. |
+| `capital_efficiency_at_32k` | 0.12 | The prize must actually reach the next milestone. |
+| `nasa_technology_basis` | 0.10 | Entries are explicitly often NASA-technology based (S2), and Startup NASA removes the up-front licence fee (S9). A documented licence is a scoring line, not decoration. |
+| `follow_on_nondilutive_ladder` | 0.10 | ExF's Capital Formation mandate means a portfolio company that goes on to win SBIR/STTR/DOE/EDA money is a reportable outcome for them. |
+| `founder_unfair_advantage` | 0.10 | Panels fund people. What does *this* entrant have that a stranger does not. |
+| `stage_demonstrability` | 0.08 | Five minutes in front of judges. What can be shown working, live. |
+| `regulatory_or_mandated_pull` | 0.06 | A mandated buyer beats a delighted one. |
+| `defensibility` | 0.04 | Real, but at pre-seed a panel discounts moat talk heavily. Deliberately the smallest weight. |
+
+Two anti-gaming rules were applied (section 9): a score of 3 or below on any
+criterion is recorded as a **catastrophic weakness** on the entrant's record and
+is never allowed to vanish into the weighted average, and rounds 2 and 3 are kept
+as separate columns rather than folded in.
+
+### 2.1 Sensitivity — where this rubric breaks
+
+`founder_unfair_advantage` at 0.10 is the criterion most open to the charge that
+it rigs the outcome toward the entrant's existing codebase. So the rubric was
+attacked directly, re-normalising the surviving weights each time. Reproduce with
+`score_tournament.py`; results are stored under `sensitivity` in
+`TOURNAMENT_RESULTS.json`.
+
+| Rubric variant | Frontier Assurance | CryoAssay | Winner | Margin |
+|---|---|---|---|---|
+| Baseline | 8.790 | 8.020 | Frontier Assurance | 0.770 |
+| Founder advantage removed | 8.656 | 8.578 | Frontier Assurance | **0.078** |
+| Capital efficiency removed | 8.625 | 8.295 | Frontier Assurance | 0.330 |
+| NASA basis doubled to 0.20, founder halved to 0.05 | 8.562 | 8.352 | Frontier Assurance | 0.210 |
+| **Both prize-physics criteria removed** | 8.449 | **8.974** | **CryoAssay** | 0.525 |
+| **Hardware-favouring rubric** (NASA 0.20, capital 0.05, founder 0.05, demo 0.04) | 8.394 | **8.628** | **CryoAssay** | 0.234 |
+
+This is the most important table in the report, and it does not say what a
+motivated author would want it to say. Removing the founder criterion alone leaves
+the winner ahead by **0.078**, which is inside the noise of any judgement-based
+scoring and should be read as a tie, not a win. Removing both prize-physics
+criteria, or adopting a rubric that rewards hardware and NASA patent licensing,
+**flips the result to CryoAssay**.
+
+The recommendation therefore rests on a single load-bearing premise: *that a
+$32,000 non-dilutive prize is scored on what the money can actually reach and on
+what the founder has already built*. That premise is defensible from the prize
+size alone, and it is why capital efficiency and founder advantage carry 0.22
+between them. But it is a premise, not a finding — which is exactly why
+obligation O2, obtaining the published rubric, is the first node in the execution
+DAG rather than a footnote.
+
+---
+
+## 3. Scouting and saturation (sections 2, 3)
+
+Search covered: the ExF programme surface and its funders; NASA Technology
+Transfer, Startup NASA and the NASA Software Catalog; NASA cryogenic fluid
+management and zero-boil-off literature; the LNG boil-off gas engineering
+literature; the Brownsville industrial corridor (Rio Grande LNG, Texas LNG, Port
+of Brownsville, Starbase); the reported AFRL offshore-platform rocket recovery
+programme; and the NASA autonomous-systems certification literature (ATTRACTOR,
+Resilient Autonomy, MM-RTA).
+
+Saturation was reached when three consecutive searches in the cryogenics and
+offshore families returned only sources already registered, and when new
+candidate ideas began arriving as variants of registered entries rather than as
+new mechanisms.
+
+**Saturation was NOT reached on the ExF-specific evidence.** Four separate
+primary-source fetches were blocked by this environment's egress proxy
+(`expandingfrontiers.org`, `exfspacetechppitchcomp2024.org`, `airforcetimes.com`).
+Per AGENTS.md courtroom rule 10 nothing was reconstructed from those pages. They
+are logged as blocking obligations O1-O7 and appear as gating nodes in the DAG.
+
+---
+
+## 4. The field (section 6)
+
+Thirty serious entrants across eight families: cryogenics (6), offshore and
+recovery (6), sensing (4), autonomy and software (5), ecosystem and workforce (2),
+materials and manufacturing (3), power (2), data and earth observation (2). Full
+per-criterion matrix in `TOURNAMENT_RESULTS.json`.
+
+**Excluded before entry**, with reasons, so the exclusions can be challenged:
+
+- Launch vehicles, satellite buses, and constellations. Capital scale is three
+  orders of magnitude past the prize; entering one signals a misread of the room.
+- Space tourism, asteroid mining, orbital data centres. No local customer, no
+  near-term revenue, and a panel of practitioners discounts them hard.
+- Pure consulting and pure services with no technology asset. ExF's mandate is
+  technology commercialisation.
+- Anything requiring an ITAR-controlled facility on day one. The prize cannot
+  reach that milestone.
+- Regolith and soil stabilisation was *kept* in the field despite being an
+  obvious loser, as a calibration control. It finished last (5.02) and was
+  eliminated, which is the behaviour a working rubric should produce.
+
+---
+
+## 5. Triple elimination (sections 7, 8)
+
+Three rounds, each a distinct question, a loss being a below-median finish:
+
+- **Round 1 — the rubric.** Weighted criteria score.
+- **Round 2 — the judging room.** How the entry survives four adversarial
+  scenarios: (a) a judge asks "why does this have to be in Brownsville";
+  (b) a judge asks "who writes you a cheque in the next twelve months";
+  (c) a judge asks "what have you actually built"; (d) a judge with deep domain
+  expertise attacks the technical premise.
+- **Round 3 — execution reality.** Can *this* entrant credibly stand behind it
+  this cycle, without a co-founder who does not yet exist.
+
+Twenty-five of thirty survived; five were eliminated on three losses. Triple
+elimination did real work: **ZBO reliquefaction skid retrofit** scored third on
+the pure rubric (7.33) and would have been a finalist under single elimination,
+but took a fatal round-3 loss (score 2) because it requires cryogenic hardware
+engineering the entrant does not have. Single elimination would have hidden that.
+
+### The decisive battles
+
+**Propellant-grade LNG assay (7.880) versus Verifiable autonomy receipts (7.870).**
+The closest matchup in the tournament, one hundredth of a point apart, and the
+two entries are near-perfect complements. The assay idea wins regional anchor
+(10 vs 6), customer proximity (10 vs 7), mission fit (10 vs 8) and regulatory
+pull (9 vs 7). The receipts idea wins capital efficiency (10 vs 6), founder
+advantage (10 vs 3) and demonstrability (10 vs 6). Neither loss is superficial:
+the assay's founder-advantage 3 is a real catastrophic weakness (no cryogenic
+credential, needs a technical co-founder before the pitch), and the receipts'
+regional-anchor 6 is a real one too (a judge can legitimately ask why this is not
+a San Francisco company). **The tournament's central finding is that each idea's
+fatal flaw is the other's strength**, which is precisely the condition that makes
+hybridisation worth attempting rather than a gimmick.
+
+**Verifiable autonomy receipts versus Autonomous flight-software V&V service.**
+Both are software-assurance plays by the same founder. V&V loses on regional
+anchor (4 vs 6) and customer proximity (5 vs 7) because its customers are
+smallsat primes in Colorado and California, not Gulf operators. Its component
+value was preserved: its NASA formal-methods lineage is the winner's route to a
+documented NASA technology basis.
+
+**Attacks on the leader, run honestly:**
+
+1. *"This is an IT product wearing a space costume."* Real risk, and the most
+   likely way this entry loses in the room. Mitigation is structural, not
+   cosmetic: the wedge must be a named uncrewed operation with a named local
+   operator, and the demo must show a sealed check catching a false success
+   claim, live. If the founder cannot name the operator by pitch day, this
+   attack lands and the entry should be swapped for CryoAssay.
+2. *"Your own README says prototype, no production use, no user validation"* (S19).
+   Correct, and it must be said out loud on stage. For a $32,000 non-dilutive
+   prize aimed at pre-seed founders this is not a weakness, it is the reason to
+   award the money. It would be fatal in a Series A room; this is not one.
+3. *"There is no NASA technology here."* The weakest point of the winner, scored
+   honestly at 7. There is no patent licence. The mitigation is real but must be
+   executed, not asserted: the NASA Software Catalog distributes formal-methods
+   and runtime-assurance tooling (PVS-based simplex runtime assurance, DAIDALUS)
+   free to US entities (S10), and NASA's own literature documents autonomy
+   certification as an open barrier (S11). Node `EF-030` exists to convert that
+   from a claim into a signed software usage agreement before submission.
+4. *"Evidence bundles are a solved problem — Sigstore, in-toto, SLSA."* Partly
+   true and the strongest technical attack. The differentiator is not the bundle
+   format, it is the **independent re-execution of a check sealed before the
+   change**, which supply-chain attestation does not do: those systems attest
+   that an artefact came from a pipeline, not that an independent party re-ran
+   the acceptance test and it passed. That distinction must survive contact with
+   a sharp judge or the entry is commodity.
+
+---
+
+## 6. Component winners and preserved ideas (section 10)
+
+| Component | Winner |
+|---|---|
+| Regional lock-in | Propellant-grade LNG assay |
+| NASA technology basis | NASA-licensed corrosion and TPS coatings |
+| Capital efficiency | Verifiable autonomy receipts |
+| Live stage demo | Verifiable autonomy receipts |
+| Regulatory pull | Methane plume detection |
+| Dual-use space-energy thesis | Propellant-grade LNG assay |
+| Follow-on funding ladder | Verifiable autonomy receipts |
+| Physical credibility on stage | Refractory and ablative pad materials |
+| Workforce and ecosystem alignment | RGV supplier readiness marketplace |
+
+Preserved from losers: the Boca Chica community-monitoring entry has the
+strongest community-benefit framing in the field and is borrowed as a slide, not
+a business. The technician-credentialing entry scores a perfect 10 on regional
+anchor and is folded into the winner as an explicit RGV hiring commitment. The
+pad-materials entry proves that physical props beat slides, so the winner brings
+a tangible artefact to the stage.
+
+---
+
+## 7. Hybrids (sections 11, 12)
+
+Four hybrids were built. They did not all win, which is the point.
+
+| Hybrid | Weighted | Outcome |
+|---|---|---|
+| **Frontier Assurance** | **8.79** | Champion. |
+| CryoAssay | 8.02 | Runner-up. |
+| Rockets and Rigs Cryo Autonomy Suite | 7.26 | **Lost.** Deliberate over-combination — receipts plus assay plus tank sensing sold as one platform. It scores well on mission fit and region and still loses, because bundling destroyed capital efficiency (4) and demonstrability (5). Breadth does not survive a five-minute pitch. |
+| Saltline | 6.84 | Third overall, but note it scores **exactly** its own core component. Adding a structural digital twin to a coatings business produced zero lift. An honest hybrid that failed to be a hybrid. |
+
+**Why Frontier Assurance gains 0.92 over its core.** The hybrid is not "receipts
+plus more features." It changes what the company is *for*: from a developer tool
+that verifies coding agents, to an assurance layer for uncrewed physical
+operations. That single reframing moves mission fit 8→9, regional anchor 6→8,
+customer proximity 7→9 and regulatory pull 7→8, while capital efficiency,
+founder advantage and demonstrability all stay at their maxima because the
+underlying machinery — sealed checks, independent re-execution, tamper-evident
+bundles — is unchanged and already built. It borrows the remote-operations-centre
+entry's Brownsville anchoring, the V&V entry's NASA formal-methods lineage, and
+the leak-localisation entry's cryogenic use case. Nothing in the borrowed set
+requires new core technology, which is why the hybrid is cheap and why the
+combination is coherent rather than decorative.
+
+**New weaknesses the hybrid introduces**, stated because hybrids usually hide
+them: it takes on a domain the founder does not have (offshore and cryogenic
+operations), so every technical claim about those environments must come from a
+design partner rather than from the founder; and it inherits a dependency on the
+reported AFRL programme (S17), which is C-confidence evidence from a single
+aggregator. If O6 fails, the offshore wedge is removed and the cryogenic-transfer
+wedge at Rio Grande LNG carries the pitch alone. The entry survives that, at a
+lower score.
+
+---
+
+## 8. Final championship (section 13)
+
+Best original: Propellant-grade LNG assay and loss accounting, 7.880.
+Best hybrid: Frontier Assurance, 8.790.
+
+Hardest scenario applied to both — *a judge who has personally run a cryogenic
+facility, plus a judge who has personally raised venture capital, attacking
+simultaneously*:
+
+The assay entry survives the operator but loses the investor: the operator asks
+who calibrates the assay and against which standard, and there is no answer
+without a co-founder; the investor asks what has been built and the answer is a
+plan. The receipts entry survives the investor easily — working code, a live
+offline demo, a deterministic re-execution — and takes damage from the operator
+on domain naivety, which is repairable inside the competition timeline by
+recruiting one design partner and quoting them.
+
+**Winner: Frontier Assurance.** The decisive factor is not technology quality; it
+is that its remaining weakness is fixable with a phone call and thirty days,
+while the runner-up's remaining weakness requires recruiting a co-founder with a
+cryogenics credential.
+
+**When the runner-up is preferable, stated plainly:**
+
+- If ExF publishes a rubric weighting NASA patent licensing or hardware above
+  founder traction (obligation O2). Not hypothetical: section 2.1 shows such a
+  rubric produces CryoAssay 8.628 against Frontier Assurance 8.394.
+- If a co-founder with genuine cryogenic or LNG operations credentials joins
+  before the deadline. That single change moves CryoAssay's founder-advantage
+  score from 3 to 8 and its total to roughly 8.5, past the winner.
+- If the AFRL programme evidence (O6) collapses *and* no cryogenic-transfer
+  design partner can be secured, removing both of the winner's physical wedges.
+
+---
+
+## 9. Final architecture of the winner
+
+**Company:** Frontier Assurance (Brownsville, Texas).
+**Product:** a sealed flight recorder for autonomous operations.
+**One-line pitch:** *Autonomy is arriving on the Gulf faster than the paperwork
+that proves it worked. We make an uncrewed system prove what it actually did, to
+a standard an inspector can re-run.*
+
+**What it technically is**, and this is the part that must be true: before an
+autonomous operation runs, the acceptance conditions are **sealed** — fixed and
+fingerprinted so they cannot be edited afterward. The operation runs. An
+independent process then **re-executes those sealed checks** against the recorded
+result, in a separate workspace, and publishes a tamper-evident bundle containing
+the commands run, their exit codes, the resulting state change, and the
+independent verdict. A failed validation publishes nothing. This is the
+machinery already implemented in this repository for software delivery
+(Explorer, Builder, Curator; `hive-mind verify`), pointed at physical operations.
+
+**Why it is dual-use, which is the whole Rockets & Rigs thesis:** an uncrewed
+offshore recovery platform and an automated cryogenic transfer at an LNG terminal
+have the same unsolved problem — the autonomous system reports success, and the
+operator, the insurer and the regulator each have to take its word for it. NASA
+has documented this as a genuine barrier to certifying autonomous systems (S11).
+Offshore energy already runs on a safety-case culture that expects auditable
+evidence. The same evidence layer serves both, and both customers are inside a
+30 km radius of Brownsville.
+
+**Beachhead:** one design partner, one operation, one sealed check, one bundle a
+regulator or insurer would accept. Not a platform. Not a suite.
+
+**Business model:** per-operation assurance subscription plus a one-time
+integration fee; expand by operation count, not by seat count.
+
+**What the $32,000 actually buys** — this is the slide that wins non-dilutive
+prizes, because it makes the money legible:
+
+| Use | Amount |
+|---|---|
+| Design-partner pilot: instrument one real local operation end to end | $14,000 |
+| NASA Software Catalog licence integration and formal-methods conformance work | $6,000 |
+| Independent third-party review of one published bundle | $5,000 |
+| Legal: entity formation, licence agreements, design-partner terms | $4,000 |
+| Travel and demonstration hardware for the pitch and follow-on meetings | $3,000 |
+
+**Follow-on ladder:** AFRL/SpaceWERX and NASA SBIR topics on trusted autonomy and
+mission assurance; DOE programmes on methane and facility safety; EDA and Texas
+Space Commission regional instruments. Each is a reportable Capital Formation
+outcome for ExF, which is exactly what their SBA award obliges them to produce
+(S6).
+
+**RGV commitment (borrowed from the credentialing entrant):** first two technical
+hires from UTRGV or Texas Southmost College, stated on the slide with numbers.
+
+**Honesty constraints that must survive into the pitch**, because breaking them
+is both wrong and, in a room of practitioners, fatal:
+
+- Say "working prototype, deterministic offline demonstration, no production
+  deployment and no user validation yet." That is what the README says (S19) and
+  a judge who clones the repository will read it.
+- Do not claim a NASA patent licence until one is signed. Say "NASA Software
+  Catalog tooling, application in progress" if that is the true state.
+- Do not present the Project Able Baker figures (S17) as fact. They are
+  single-aggregator sourced. Say "reported" or verify them first via O6.
+- Do not claim the evidence format is novel against Sigstore, in-toto or SLSA.
+  Claim the independent re-execution of a pre-sealed check, which is the part
+  that is actually different.
+
+---
+
+## 10. Unknowns
+
+1. The real ExF rubric and deadline (O1, O2). Everything is scheduled off these.
+2. Whether the 2026 prize is still $32,000 and how it splits (O3).
+3. Eligibility mechanics: incorporation, residency, stage limits, re-entry (O4).
+4. Prior winners, which reveal panel preference better than any rubric (O5).
+5. Whether the AFRL offshore recovery programme carries a real autonomy-assurance
+   requirement (O6).
+6. Whether a specific NASA Software Catalog item or Startup NASA patent is
+   licensable for this concept and on what terms (O7).
+7. Whether a Brownsville design partner will sign inside the competition
+   timeline. This is the single highest-variance unknown in the plan, and node
+   `EF-040` is the go/no-go on it.
+
+---
+
+## 11. What would change this answer
+
+State the falsifiers up front, so the recommendation can be killed cleanly:
+
+- ExF publishes a rubric that weights hardware or a NASA patent licence above
+  capital efficiency and traction → switch to CryoAssay.
+- No Brownsville design partner signs within 30 days → the winner has no wedge
+  and drops behind CryoAssay and Saltline.
+- A cryogenics co-founder joins → CryoAssay overtakes the winner outright.
+- The competition requires a formed Texas entity with revenue → re-score the
+  whole field on eligibility before anything else.

+# User Objective and Session Directives
+
+## Original subject supplied
+
+> Use hive-mind-os on a new branch from latest main to find me top 3 ideas to
+> compete and put into https://www.expandingfrontiers.org
+>
+> Just use the subject dag to come up with best winner on idea to get a grant or award.
+
+## SUBJECT as interpreted
+
+> Identify the venture idea most likely to WIN a grant or award from Expanding
+> Frontiers (ExF), the Brownsville, Texas 501(c)(3) space-and-energy innovation
+> ecosystem builder, and produce the top three entries plus an executable plan
+> for the winner.
+
+## Governing interpretation
+
+1. **The objective is winning, not being interesting.** The scoring system is
+   derived from what ExF is actually rewarded for as a nonprofit ecosystem
+   builder (regional job creation, NASA technology commercialization, the
+   space-energy crossover thesis), not from generic venture-capital criteria.
+   An idea that a Sand Hill Road partner would fund and an ExF judging panel
+   would pass over is a losing entry here.
+2. **Non-dilutive prize scale sets the physics.** The flagship ExF Space Tech
+   Pitch Competition awards a reported $32,000 total across the best three
+   business plans. Capital efficiency is therefore a first-class criterion: an
+   idea whose next honest milestone costs $2M cannot be de-risked by this prize
+   and scores badly no matter how good the technology is.
+3. **Geography is a scoring dimension, not background.** ExF's own funding
+   (EDA STEM Challenge, DOE EPIC Prize, SBA Growth Accelerator Fund) is
+   justified on Rio Grande Valley economic development. An idea that could be
+   executed from anywhere is worth materially less to them than one that must
+   be executed within 30 km of Brownsville.
+4. **Evidence discipline applies (AGENTS.md courtroom rule).** Several primary
+   sources were unreachable from this environment. Nothing from a blocked
+   source is invented. Each such item is recorded as a blocking evidence
+   obligation in `SOURCE_REGISTER.md` and carried into the execution DAG as a
+   node the founder must discharge before submitting.
+5. **The founder's existing assets are part of the field.** This repository is
+   a real, working, differentiated asset owned by the entrant. Ignoring it
+   would have been an analytical error; overstating its maturity would have
+   been a dishonest one. It is entered as a competitor and judged like every
+   other entrant, including on its README's own admission of prototype status.
+
+## Method
+
+The repository's own `prompts/shared/ULTIMATE_SOLUTION_TOURNAMENT.md`
+(GenericPrompt) was executed against the SUBJECT: dynamic criteria construction
+(section 4), a 30-entrant field (section 6), triple-elimination scoring
+(section 7), adversarial attack on leaders (section 8), component-level winners
+(section 10), hybrid challengers (section 11), and a final championship
+(section 13), followed by the Part II conversion of the winner into a
+machine-readable execution DAG with node contracts (section 17).

+"""Validate EXECUTION_DAG.json: dependency resolution, acyclicity, level ordering,
+durability ordering for irreversible nodes, critical-path integrity, and presence of
+every GenericPrompt section 17 node-contract field.
+
+Run: python docs/plan/expanding-frontiers-tournament-2026-08-28/validate_dag.py
+Exit 0 = valid. Exit 1 = errors printed.
+"""
+
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+import json
+import pathlib
+import sys
+
+CONTRACT_FIELDS = [
+    "id", "objective", "rationale", "dependencies", "assumptions", "required_inputs",
+    "expected_outputs", "read_scope", "write_scope", "forbidden_scope", "branch",
+    "acceptance_criteria", "evidence_requirements", "risk", "reversibility", "effort",
+    "critical_path_importance", "downstream_unlock_value", "merge_conflict_surface",
+    "file_locks", "semantic_locks", "parallel_safe", "rollback", "stopping_condition",
+    "escalation_conditions", "min_openai_model", "min_anthropic_model",
+]
+
+
+def main() -> int:
+    plan = json.loads((pathlib.Path(__file__).with_name("EXECUTION_DAG.json")).read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
+    nodes = {n["id"]: n for n in plan["nodes"]}
+    errors: list[str] = []
+
+    level_of = {i: int(l.split("_")[1]) for l, ids in plan["safe_parallelism"].items() for i in ids}
+    if set(level_of) != set(nodes):
+        errors.append(f"level coverage mismatch: {sorted(set(nodes) ^ set(level_of))}")
+
+    seen: set[str] = set()
+    stack: set[str] = set()
+
+    def visit(nid: str) -> None:
+        if nid in stack:
+            errors.append(f"cycle detected at {nid}")
+            return
+        if nid in seen:
+            return
+        stack.add(nid)
+        for dep in nodes[nid]["dependencies"]:
+            if dep in nodes:
+                visit(dep)
+        stack.discard(nid)
+        seen.add(nid)
+
+    for nid in nodes:
+        visit(nid)
+
+    for nid, node in nodes.items():
+        for dep in node["dependencies"]:
+            if dep not in nodes:
+                errors.append(f"{nid}: unknown dependency {dep}")
+            elif level_of.get(dep, -1) >= level_of.get(nid, 99):
+                errors.append(f"{nid} (L{level_of.get(nid)}) depends on {dep} (L{level_of.get(dep)}); a dependency level is not an executable wave")
+        if node["reversibility"] == "irreversible" and len(plan["safe_parallelism"][f"level_{level_of[nid]}"]) != 1:
+            errors.append(f"{nid} is irreversible but shares its level with other nodes")
+        for field in CONTRACT_FIELDS:
+            if field not in node:
+                errors.append(f"{nid}: missing section-17 contract field {field}")
+
+    path = plan["critical_path"]
+    for earlier, later in zip(path, path[1:]):
+        if earlier not in nodes[later]["dependencies"]:
+            errors.append(f"critical path is not a chain: {later} does not depend on {earlier}")
+
+    if errors:
+        print("DAG INVALID")
+        for error in errors:
+            print(f"  - {error}")
+        return 1
+
+    print(f"DAG VALID: {len(nodes)} nodes, {len(plan['safe_parallelism'])} levels, critical path {' -> '.join(path)}")
+    return 0
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    sys.exit(main())

+# DO THIS NEXT
+
+Two tracks. They are independent, so the student never waits on the venture.
+
+---
+
+## Before anything: the call that can kill this
+
+**One conversation with Expanding Frontiers, three questions.** These are nodes
+`WS-000`, `WS-001` and `YM-000`, and any of them can end the plan, which is why they
+come first.
+
+1. *"Is anyone already doing calibrated community overpressure or noise monitoring at
+   a spaceport? Airports all do it. Do you know of a spaceport that does?"* ExF sits
+   inside this ecosystem. If anyone knows, they do. **If the answer is yes, both
+   winners collapse and the answer becomes Peninsula.**
+2. *"Would you see an independent launch-impact measurement venture as coexistence
+   infrastructure for the ecosystem, or as adversarial to it?"* Ask it in those words.
+   Do not guess. If they hear it as adversarial, keep the idea and change the venue.
+3. *"For the Space Entrepreneur Summer Academy: what are the 2026 dates and deadline,
+   and do students bring their own project or get assigned one?"* The youth plan
+   depends entirely on the last part.
+
+The heaviest criterion in the whitespace tournament, at 0.20, is scored from failing
+to find a competitor in a web search. That is the weakest evidence in this document
+and the claim most likely to be wrong. `WS-000` exists to attack it properly: USPTO,
+SBIR and STTR awards, Crunchbase, trade press, FAA and Cameron County filings, plus
+that question to ExF.
+
+---
+
+## Venture track — Boom Baseline
+
+**Session 1 (nodes WS-000, WS-001, WS-002).** Sonnet-class, medium effort.
+
+> Read `docs/plan/expanding-frontiers-whitespace-and-youth-2026-08-28/SOURCE_REGISTER.md`
+> and `EXECUTION_DAG_VENTURE.json`. Execute WS-000, WS-001 and WS-002 in parallel.
+> WS-000 is the important one: your job is to DISPROVE the claim that nobody is doing
+> calibrated community overpressure monitoring at a spaceport. Search USPTO, SBIR and
+> STTR award databases, Crunchbase, aerospace and acoustics trade press, FAA
+> environmental filings and Cameron County records. Produce
+> `WHITESPACE_VERIFICATION.md`. Record negative results as "searched X, Y, Z and found
+> nothing", never as "nobody is doing this". If you find a competitor, say so plainly
+> and do not defend the recommendation. Stop there. Write no pitch and no plan.
+
+**Session 2 (WS-010).** Opus-class, high effort. Lock the entry and venue, re-running
+`score_tournaments.py` with any corrected inputs. This node is allowed to overturn the
+winner.
+
+**Then WS-020 first and hardest.** Find one payer who will state in writing what they
+would pay. This is the weakest part of the whole idea, stated honestly: airports fund
+their own monitoring, and the analogous payer here is unconfirmed. If no payer exists
+after 30 days, that is a real finding — it means this is a public-good programme and a
+student project rather than a venture, and saying so is better than pitching a
+business with no buyer.
+
+`WS-030` (consent and privacy) runs in parallel and is not optional. Publishing
+measurements about identifiable homes without a policy is how this goes wrong.
+
+---
+
+## Youth track — The Boom Map
+
+Runs independently. A student can start `YM-010` the day `YM-000` answers.
+
+**The order matters and is deliberate: the consent protocol is written before the
+first sensor is built.** Not bureaucracy. It is what makes the project defensible, and
+a judging panel will notice that a sixteen-year-old thought about consent before
+hardware.
+
+1. **`YM-000`** — SESA dates, deadline, and whether students bring their own project.
+   Conrad Challenge and Diamond Challenge as alternates; the same work fits all three
+   with no rework.
+2. **`YM-010`** — one page: homeowner consent, parental consent, school permission,
+   and a publication policy that never identifies an address.
+3. **`YM-020`** — build three nodes, starting on your own house, and calibrate them
+   against each other. Under $500 total. Write the build guide as you go.
+4. **`YM-030`** — recruit twelve to fifteen homes plus the school. Eight is the floor.
+   Spread them by distance; the gradient is the science.
+5. **`YM-040`** — capture a launch, publish the map, the method, the limitations and
+   the raw data.
+6. **`YM-050`** — submit.
+
+**The pitch is one sentence:** *every airport measures its noise, no spaceport does,
+so I built the first one.*
+
+---
+
+## Hard stops, both tracks
+
+- **Never claim causation.** The data measures what arrived at a house. It does not
+  measure what caused a crack. Say that out loud, in the pitch and in the writeup. It
+  is both the honest position and the credible one.
+- **Never build a plaintiff-side business.** Same data, same terms, to every party
+  including the operator. The moment it serves one side, its value is gone.
+- **Never publish an address.** Aggregate by street or larger, with written consent
+  before installation.
+- **Do not say "nobody is doing this"** until `WS-000` is done. Say "we searched these
+  places and found nothing."
+- **Do not put a minor near cryogens, rocket hardware, industrial property or a
+  wildlife refuge permit.** Every node in the youth track is designed to avoid this.
+- **Do not lead the sargassum idea with the yield.** Lead with the arsenic. Methane
+  yield is modest and the contamination is real; a judge who knows the field will ask,
+  and having asked it first is the difference between credible and not.
+

+python docs/plan/expanding-frontiers-whitespace-and-youth-2026-08-28/validate_dag.py
